questions.text: On which type of stage does the audience sit on every side of the acting area?

options: Proscenium arch
In the round
Thrust
End-on
feedback: A thrust stage has the audience on three sides, not all of them

questions.solution: In-the-round staging has the audience surrounding the acting area on all sides
questions.hint: Picture a boxing ring with seats on every side of it

questions.text: Which type of stage has the audience seated on three sides of the acting area? Give the term.

feedback.traverse: Traverse staging has the audience on two opposite sides
feedback.in the round: In the round has the audience on all four sides

questions.solution: A thrust stage juts out into the audience, who sit on three sides of it
questions.hint: The stage pushes forward into the audience; the back wall is the only side without seats

questions.text: On stage, which direction is upstage?

options: Towards the back, away from the audience
Towards the front, nearest the audience
To the actor's left as they face the audience
To the actor's right as they face the audience
feedback: That is downstage, the part nearest the audience

questions.solution: Upstage is the back of the stage, furthest from the audience; downstage is the front
questions.hint: On old sloping stages, the back of the stage was higher than the front

questions.text: Who has the overall artistic vision for a production, interprets the script and leads the actors in rehearsals? Give the job title.

feedback.stage manager: The stage manager organises rehearsals and runs the show backstage, but does not set the artistic vision
feedback.producer: The producer looks after money and the business side of a production

questions.solution: The director decides how the play will be interpreted and guides the actors and designers towards that vision
questions.hint: This person gives the actors notes and decides how each scene is staged

questions.text: What are the wings of a stage?

options: The space above the stage where scenery is hung
The part of the stage in front of the curtain
The seating area for the audience
The hidden offstage areas at the sides of the stage
feedback: That is the apron
That is the auditorium

questions.solution: The wings are the offstage spaces to the left and right of the acting area, hidden from the audience
questions.hint: Think of where a bird's wings are on its body

questions.text: Which member of a theatre company writes the script of a new play?

options: Director
Playwright
Producer
Stage manager

questions.solution: The playwright writes the script; 'wright' is an old word for a maker, as in shipwright
questions.hint: The job title ends with an old word meaning a maker

questions.text: What is the name of the frame around the opening of a traditional stage, through which the audience watches the action like a picture? Give the term.
questions.solution: The proscenium arch frames the stage like a picture frame, with the audience on one side
questions.hint: The term starts with P and comes from an ancient Greek word meaning 'in front of the scene'

questions.text: Which staging has the audience on two opposite sides, facing each other, with the acting area between them?

options: Thrust
Traverse
In the round
End-on
feedback: A thrust stage has the audience on three sides

questions.solution: In traverse staging the audience sit on two sides facing each other, like at a catwalk show
questions.hint: Think of a fashion catwalk

questions.text: What is the difference between thrust and traverse staging?

options: Thrust has the audience on three sides; traverse has it on two opposite sides
Thrust has the audience on two opposite sides; traverse has it on three sides
Thrust has the audience on all four sides; traverse has it on one side
Thrust has the audience on one side; traverse has it on all four sides
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: A thrust stage has audience on three sides; traverse staging has audience on two opposite sides
questions.hint: Picture a stage pushed out into the seats, then a catwalk

questions.text: An actor faces the audience and walks towards their own left. Which direction are they moving?

options: Stage right
House left
Stage left
Downstage
feedback: Stage right is the actor's right-hand side
House left is the audience's left, which is the actor's right

questions.solution: Stage left and stage right are given from the actor's point of view as they face the audience
questions.hint: Stage directions are given from the actor's point of view, not the audience's

questions.text: Which member of the production team runs the backstage crew and makes sure each performance runs smoothly once the show has opened? Give the job title.

feedback.director: The director's main work is in rehearsals; once the show is running, someone else keeps each performance on track
feedback.producer: The producer looks after money and the business side, not the running of each show

questions.solution: The stage manager supervises the crew and the running of every performance, keeping the show as it was rehearsed
questions.hint: This person is in charge backstage night after night during the run

questions.text: What is the apron of a stage?

options: The part of the stage in front of the main curtain, closest to the audience
The space above the stage where scenery is raised
The sloping floor under the audience seating
A rotating section of the stage floor
feedback: That is the fly tower (the flies)
That describes raked audience seating, not part of the stage
That is a revolve

questions.solution: The apron extends in front of the curtain line or proscenium arch, nearest the audience
questions.hint: Like an apron you wear, it is at the front

questions.text: What is the main difference between a producer and a director in theatre?

options: The producer manages money and business matters; the director leads the artistic side and rehearsals
The producer leads rehearsals; the director raises the money
The producer writes the script; the director builds the set
The producer operates the lights; the director operates the sound
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: The producer handles finance, budgets and business; the director shapes the artistic interpretation and runs rehearsals
questions.hint: One role is about the business, the other about the art

questions.text: What is the name for the part of a theatre where the audience sits to watch the play? Give the term.

feedback.foyer: The foyer is the entrance area where the audience gathers before the show

questions.solution: The audience sits in the auditorium, also called the house
questions.hint: The word comes from the Latin verb meaning 'to hear'

questions.text: What is the name for a section of the stage floor that turns round to change the scene quickly? Give the term.
questions.solution: A revolve is a turntable built into the stage floor that rotates scenery and actors
questions.hint: It begins with R and spins like a record player

questions.text: A set designer is told that nothing taller than a chair can stand anywhere in the acting area, because it would block someone's view wherever it was placed. Which stage type is the production using?

options: Thrust
Traverse
In the round
Proscenium arch
feedback: A thrust stage has a back wall where tall scenery can go
Traverse staging has two open ends where tall scenery can go
A proscenium stage can have tall scenery at the back

questions.solution: In the round, every part of the acting area is seen from all sides, so tall scenery would always block someone's view
questions.hint: Which stage has no 'back' where tall scenery could stand?

questions.text: Priya is standing downstage centre. The director asks her to move as far from the audience as she can without moving left or right. Where does she end up?

options: Downstage left
Upstage centre
Centre stage right
Upstage right

questions.solution: Moving away from the audience is moving upstage; keeping her left–right position keeps her in the centre: upstage centre
questions.hint: Moving away from the audience means moving 'up' the stage

questions.text: A company performs a play set in a factory inside a real empty factory, chosen because the building suits the story. What is this type of theatre called? Give the term.

feedback.promenade: Promenade means the audience moves around to follow the action; the key point here is the real location chosen for the story

questions.solution: Site-specific theatre is performed in a real place outside a theatre, chosen because it fits the play
questions.hint: Think about where the performance takes place and why that place was picked

questions.text: During the run of a play, a lead actor is too ill to perform. Who is ready to take over the role because they have learned it in advance?

options: The dresser
The stage manager
The prompter
The understudy
feedback: A dresser helps actors with their costumes

questions.solution: An understudy learns a role so they can perform it if the usual actor cannot
questions.hint: This performer studies the part in case they are needed

questions.text: The audience walks with the actors from room to room in an old house, following the action from scene to scene. What type of staging is this?

options: Traverse
Promenade
Thrust
End-on

questions.solution: In promenade staging the audience moves around to follow the action
questions.hint: The name comes from the French for 'a walk'

questions.text: A director tells an actor to cross from upstage right to the stage position diagonally opposite. Where should the actor finish? Give the stage position.

feedback.downstage right: That only changes upstage to downstage; diagonally opposite also swaps right and left
feedback.upstage left: That only swaps right and left; diagonally opposite also swaps upstage and downstage

questions.solution: Diagonally opposite swaps both parts of the position: upstage becomes downstage and right becomes left
questions.hint: Change both parts of the position, not just one

questions.text: Read this description of a performance space: 'The seats are all on one side. There is no frame around the stage, and the front row sits level with the edge of the acting area.' Which stage type is described?

options: End-on
Proscenium arch
Thrust
Traverse
feedback: A proscenium stage has a frame (the arch) around it
A thrust stage has the audience on three sides

questions.solution: Audience on one side only, with no arch framing the stage, is end-on staging
questions.hint: First count the sides with seats, then check whether there is a frame

questions.text: A theatre's ground plan shows the audience on three sides and a solid wall behind the stage. The designer wants a tall doorway that every audience member can see past. Where should it go?

options: Upstage, against the back wall
Downstage centre
Downstage left
In the middle of the acting area

questions.solution: On a thrust stage the back wall is the only side with no audience, so tall pieces go upstage against it
questions.hint: Which part of the stage has no audience behind it?

questions.text: From the audience's point of view, where is upstage right?

options: At the back, on the audience's right
At the front, on the audience's left
At the back, on the audience's left
At the front, on the audience's right
feedback: Stage right is the actor's right, and the actor faces the audience, so it is the audience's left
Upstage is the back of the stage, not the front

questions.solution: Upstage is the back. Stage right is the actor's right as they face the audience, which is the audience's left
questions.hint: First decide back or front, then remember that stage left and right are the actor's

questions.text: A ground plan shows two blocks of seats facing each other with a long, narrow acting area between them. Which staging challenge will the director face most often?

options: Tall scenery at the back will block every seat
The audience will have to walk between scenes
Actors will often have their backs or sides to one block of the audience
The proscenium arch will hide actors at the sides
feedback: Traverse staging has no back wall; scenery can stand at the open ends
That describes promenade staging
Traverse staging has no proscenium arch

questions.solution: This is traverse staging: with audience on two sides, actors must keep turning so neither side sees only their backs
questions.hint: Name the staging first, then think about which way the actors face

questions.text: Read this: 'Scenery is hung on bars and raised out of sight into the tall space above the stage.' What is that space above the stage called? Give the term.

feedback.wings: The wings are at the sides of the stage; this space is above it

questions.solution: Scenery is 'flown' up into the flies, the tall fly tower above the stage
questions.hint: Look upwards: this scenery travels vertically out of sight

questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of staging a play in the round.

rubric.model_answer: Advantage: every audience member is close to the action, which creates an intimate, involving experience. Disadvantage: some of the audience will always see an actor's back, so the director must keep actors moving and turning, and tall scenery cannot be used because it would block sightlines.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a valid advantage (e.g. intimacy, closeness, audience feels involved)
1 mark: the advantage explained
1 mark: a valid disadvantage (e.g. actors' backs to some seats, sightlines, no tall set)
1 mark: the disadvantage explained

questions.solution: In the round gives closeness and intimacy, but makes sightlines and set design harder
questions.hint: Think about how close the audience is and what each section of seats can see

questions.text: Which statement about the proscenium arch stage is accurate?

options: It places the audience on three sides of the acting area
It frames the action like a picture, which suits naturalistic plays that keep a 'fourth wall'
It makes it impossible to use tall scenery
It was the usual stage of ancient Greek open-air theatres
feedback: That describes a thrust stage
Tall scenery is easy to place at the back of a proscenium stage
Ancient Greek open-air theatres had no proscenium arch; it came much later

questions.solution: The proscenium arch frames the stage like a picture; with the audience on one side it suits the illusion of a 'fourth wall'
questions.hint: Think about where the audience sits and what the arch does visually

questions.text: Why do many older theatres have a raked stage that slopes upwards towards the back?

options: So that rainwater drains off the stage
So the audience can see actors at the back of the stage more clearly
So that actors can slide on and off quickly
So that the orchestra can sit underneath it

questions.solution: A raked stage improves sightlines: actors further back stand higher. This is why the back is called upstage
questions.hint: Think about what the people in the front seats can see

questions.text: Which statement about promenade staging is accurate?

options: The audience stays seated on two sides of a long acting area
It can only take place inside a proscenium arch theatre
The audience moves to follow the action, so the director must guide where they stand and look
The actors stay still while the audience watches from fixed seats
feedback: That describes traverse staging

questions.solution: In promenade staging the audience moves, so the director must guide their focus and movement through the space
questions.hint: Remember what the audience does in a promenade performance

questions.text: A director wants the audience to feel as if they are secretly watching a real family through an invisible wall. Which stage type suits this, and why?

options: In the round, because the audience surrounds the action on every side
Promenade, because the audience walks among the actors
Traverse, because the two halves of the audience can see each other across the stage
Proscenium arch, because the frame creates a clear 'fourth wall' between audience and action
feedback: Being surrounded by the audience makes an invisible wall hard to imagine
When the audience walks among the actors, there is no wall between them
The two halves of the audience see each other across the stage, which breaks the illusion

questions.solution: The invisible wall is the 'fourth wall'; a proscenium arch keeps the audience on one side, framed off from the action
questions.hint: Which stage keeps the audience on one side, behind a frame?

questions.text: Explain why the stage manager, rather than the director, is usually in charge of each performance once a show has opened.

rubric.model_answer: The director's main job is in rehearsals: shaping the interpretation, the blocking and the performances. Once the show opens, the director often moves on. The stage manager and their team run every performance, oversee the cues and the crew, and make sure the show stays as it was rehearsed, so the stage manager is in charge night after night.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: the director's main work happens in rehearsal
1 mark: the director often leaves once the show has opened
1 mark: the stage manager runs each performance and supervises the crew and cues
1 mark: the stage manager keeps the show consistent with what was rehearsed

questions.solution: The director's work is mainly in rehearsal; the stage manager runs each performance and keeps it as rehearsed
questions.hint: Compare when each person does most of their work

questions.text: Which Russian practitioner developed a 'system' to train actors to create believable, truthful characters? Give the surname.

feedback.Strasberg: Lee Strasberg was an American teacher who developed 'the Method' from the Russian practitioner's ideas

questions.solution: Konstantin Stanislavski developed his system for truthful, realistic acting
questions.hint: He co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898

questions.text: Which practitioner is most closely linked with epic theatre?

options: Konstantin Stanislavski
Antonin Artaud
Bertolt Brecht
Augusto Boal
feedback: Stanislavski is linked with naturalism and truthful acting
Artaud is linked with the Theatre of Cruelty
Augusto Boal is linked with Forum Theatre and the Theatre of the Oppressed

questions.solution: Bertolt Brecht developed epic theatre to make audiences think critically about society
questions.hint: He was a German playwright and director who founded the Berliner Ensemble

questions.text: Antonin Artaud is known for which style of theatre?

options: Epic theatre
Naturalism
Commedia dell'arte
Theatre of Cruelty

questions.solution: Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty aimed to shock the audience's senses
questions.hint: His theatre aimed to assault the senses

questions.text: Brecht used techniques to stop the audience becoming emotionally absorbed in the story, so that they would think critically about it. What is this effect usually called in English? Give the term.
questions.solution: Brecht's alienation (distancing) effect, Verfremdungseffekt in German, keeps the audience thinking rather than feeling
questions.hint: Its name suggests making the familiar seem strange

questions.text: Which theatre company is known for physical theatre exercises such as Chair Duets and Hymn Hands?

options: Complicité
Frantic Assembly
The Berliner Ensemble
The Moscow Art Theatre
feedback: Complicité is also a physical theatre company, but these exercises come from another company
The Berliner Ensemble was Brecht's company
The Moscow Art Theatre was Stanislavski's company

questions.solution: Frantic Assembly, a British physical theatre company, uses exercises such as Chair Duets and Hymn Hands
questions.hint: It is a British company known for movement-based work

questions.text: In commedia dell'arte, which stock character is a mischievous, acrobatic servant in a diamond-patterned costume?

options: Pantalone
Arlecchino (Harlequin)
Il Dottore
Il Capitano
feedback: Pantalone is the greedy old merchant
Il Dottore is the pompous doctor or scholar
Il Capitano is the boastful, cowardly soldier

questions.solution: Arlecchino (Harlequin) is the nimble, mischievous servant in a patched, diamond-patterned costume
questions.hint: In English this character's name is Harlequin

questions.text: What name is given to theatre that uses the exact words of real people, taken from interviews or records, as its script? Give the term.
questions.solution: Verbatim theatre builds its script from the recorded words of real people
questions.hint: The word is Latin for 'word for word'

questions.text: Which description matches naturalism?

options: Theatre that tries to create a detailed, believable illusion of real life on stage
Theatre that keeps reminding the audience they are watching a play
Theatre that uses masks and improvised comic routines
Theatre that attacks the audience's senses with sound and light
feedback: That describes Brecht's epic theatre
That describes commedia dell'arte
That describes Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty

questions.solution: Naturalism tries to recreate real life on stage as believably as possible
questions.hint: Think about the word 'natural'

questions.text: What did Stanislavski mean by the 'magic if'?

options: Actors imagine the audience is not there
Actors ask: 'What would I do if I were in this character's situation?'
Actors perform a scene as if it were a dream
Actors improvise a new ending to the play

questions.solution: The 'magic if' asks the actor how they would behave if they were in the character's circumstances
questions.hint: It is a question an actor asks about themselves and the character

questions.text: In Stanislavski's system, what is the term for what a character wants or is trying to achieve in a scene? Give the term.

feedback.super-objective: The super-objective is the character's overall aim across the whole play; in a single scene it is something smaller

questions.solution: A character's objective is what they want in a scene; the super-objective is their aim across the whole play
questions.hint: It is what the character is trying to get or do

questions.text: What is the main difference between Stanislavski's and Brecht's aims for the audience?

options: Stanislavski wanted the audience to think critically; Brecht wanted them to empathise
Both wanted the audience to forget they were in a theatre
Stanislavski wanted the audience to believe and empathise; Brecht wanted them to think critically
Both wanted to shock the audience's senses with sound and light
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: Stanislavski aimed for belief and empathy; Brecht aimed for critical distance
questions.hint: One wanted the audience to feel, the other wanted them to think

questions.text: In commedia dell'arte, what is the name for a rehearsed comic routine or piece of 'business' that can be slotted into a performance? Give the term.
questions.solution: Lazzi (singular lazzo) are rehearsed comic routines that commedia performers slot into the action
questions.hint: It is an Italian word beginning with L

questions.text: Which statement describes physical theatre?

options: A style that tells the story mainly through movement and the body
A style that uses only the exact words of real people
A style in which actors read the script while seated
A style that recreates real life in detailed rooms
feedback: That describes verbatim theatre
That describes a rehearsed reading, where movement is kept to a minimum
That describes naturalism

questions.solution: Physical theatre puts movement and the body at the centre of storytelling
questions.hint: Think about what the word 'physical' refers to

questions.text: Which French practitioner wrote 'The Theatre and Its Double' and wanted theatre to shock the audience's senses? Give the surname.

feedback.Brecht: Brecht was German and wanted audiences to think calmly and critically

questions.solution: Antonin Artaud set out his Theatre of Cruelty in The Theatre and Its Double (1938)
questions.hint: He was a French actor, poet and director of the 1920s and 1930s

questions.text: An actor steps out of a scene, holds up a placard saying 'Ten years later', and speaks directly to the audience. Which practitioner's techniques is this most like?

options: Konstantin Stanislavski
Antonin Artaud
Lee Strasberg
Bertolt Brecht

questions.solution: Placards and direct address are Brechtian techniques that remind the audience they are watching a play
questions.hint: Which practitioner wanted to break the illusion of reality?

questions.text: Before a scene, an actor recalls a time she felt nervous herself, to bring real feeling to her character's nerves. Which Stanislavski technique is she using?

options: Gestus
Emotion memory
Lazzi
Alienation effect
feedback: Gestus is a Brechtian gesture that shows social attitude
Lazzi are comic routines from commedia dell'arte
The alienation effect is Brecht's way of stopping the audience feeling with a character

questions.solution: Emotion memory means using a real memory of a similar feeling to make the emotion truthful
questions.hint: She is drawing on her own past feelings

questions.text: In a Brechtian performance, one actor plays several different characters and changes role in front of the audience. What is this technique called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Multi-role means one actor playing several characters, often changing role openly
questions.hint: The term describes having more than one part

questions.text: Two performers repeat a short sequence of lifts, leans and touches on and around two chairs, building a relationship without words. Whose exercise is this?

options: The Moscow Art Theatre
The Berliner Ensemble
Antonin Artaud
Frantic Assembly

questions.solution: This is Frantic Assembly's Chair Duets exercise
questions.hint: Think of the British physical theatre company

questions.text: A director stages a play in a realistic room with real furniture, and the actors never acknowledge the audience. Which style is this?

options: Epic theatre
Naturalism
Theatre of Cruelty
Commedia dell'arte
feedback: Epic theatre deliberately reminds the audience they are in a theatre
Theatre of Cruelty attacks the senses rather than recreating real life
Commedia dell'arte uses masks and stock characters, not realistic rooms

questions.solution: Realistic sets and a firm 'fourth wall' are features of naturalism
questions.hint: The aim is to look like real life

questions.text: An actor playing a greedy landlord rubs his hands while counting coins, showing his attitude to money and power in one clear gesture. What is Brecht's term for this? Give the term.
questions.solution: Gestus is Brecht's term for a gesture or movement that shows a character's social attitude
questions.hint: It is a Latin-looking word close to a common English word for a movement of the hands

questions.text: Read this description: 'Performers wear half-masks, play fixed stock characters such as a greedy old merchant and a boastful soldier, and improvise around an outline plot.' Which style is described?

options: Naturalism
Verbatim theatre
Epic theatre
Commedia dell'arte

questions.solution: Half-masks, stock characters (Pantalone, Il Capitano) and improvisation around a scenario are features of commedia dell'arte
questions.hint: Think of the Italian style from the 1500s

questions.text: A director wants the audience to leave arguing about the unfairness shown in a play rather than crying about the characters. Which practitioner's aims match this, and why?

options: Stanislavski, because he wanted audiences to believe completely in the characters
Artaud, because he wanted to overwhelm the audience's senses
Brecht, because he wanted audiences to think critically about society
Strasberg, because he wanted actors to use their own memories on screen

questions.solution: Brecht wanted audiences to judge what they saw and think about how society could change
questions.hint: Which practitioner wanted thinking rather than feeling?

questions.text: Read this note: 'The audience is surrounded by sound; there is screaming, sudden bright light and almost no dialogue.' Which practitioner's ideas does this production follow? Give the surname.

feedback.Brecht: Brecht wanted calm, critical thinking, not sensory shock
feedback.Stanislavski: Stanislavski aimed for truthful, realistic acting

questions.solution: Surrounding the audience and attacking the senses with sound and light are features of Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty
questions.hint: Think of the practitioner who wanted to assault the senses

questions.text: Which pair correctly matches a practitioner with one of their ideas?

options: Brecht: emotion memory
Artaud: the magic if
Stanislavski: given circumstances
Stanislavski: placards

questions.solution: Given circumstances are part of Stanislavski's system; emotion memory and the magic if are his too, placards are Brecht's
questions.hint: Check each idea against the practitioner who wanted truthful, realistic acting

questions.text: Before rehearsals, an actor writes down everything the script tells her about her character's age, home, time period and situation. In Stanislavski's system, what is she gathering?

options: The given circumstances
The super-objective
The alienation effect
The gestus
feedback: The super-objective is the character's overall aim, not the facts of their situation
The alienation effect is Brecht's technique, not part of Stanislavski's system
Gestus is Brecht's term for a gesture that shows social attitude

questions.solution: The given circumstances are the facts of the character's world set by the script
questions.hint: These are facts that the playwright has 'given'

questions.text: Explain two ways a director could use Brecht's techniques to stop the audience becoming emotionally absorbed in a scene.

rubric.model_answer: First, an actor could step out of role and speak directly to the audience, reminding them they are watching a play and inviting them to judge the action. Second, placards or projected captions could announce what is about to happen, removing suspense so the audience focuses on why it happens rather than what happens.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first valid technique (e.g. direct address, placards, multi-role, songs, visible scene changes)
1 mark: how it distances the audience
1 mark: second valid technique
1 mark: how it distances the audience

questions.solution: Direct address, placards, songs, multi-role and visible scene changes all break the illusion
questions.hint: Think of techniques that remind the audience they are in a theatre

questions.text: Which statement about Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty is accurate?

options: It required actors to use the exact words of real people
It was mainly about showing graphic violence on stage
It was designed to make audiences think calmly and logically about politics
It aimed to shock the audience's senses through sound, light and movement, not necessarily through violence
feedback: That describes verbatim theatre
For Artaud, 'cruelty' meant an intense assault on the senses, not simply violence
That describes Brecht's aims

questions.solution: For Artaud, 'cruelty' meant an intense assault on the senses, not simply violence
questions.hint: Think about what Artaud meant by 'cruelty'

questions.text: Why did Brecht use songs that interrupt the action?

options: To make the play feel as realistic as possible
To break the audience's emotional involvement and comment on the action
To give the actors a rest between scenes
To hide scene changes from the audience

questions.solution: Brecht's songs interrupt the story and comment on it, keeping the audience thinking
questions.hint: Think about the effect of an interruption on the audience's feelings

questions.text: A student says: 'Naturalism and Stanislavski are the same thing.' Which statement is the most accurate correction?

options: Stanislavski's system supports truthful acting in naturalistic plays, but naturalism is a wider style
Stanislavski invented epic theatre, not naturalism
Naturalism was invented by Brecht to criticise Stanislavski
Stanislavski only worked on commedia dell'arte

questions.solution: Naturalism is a whole style of theatre; Stanislavski's system is an acting approach closely linked with it
questions.hint: One is a style of theatre, the other is a method of acting

questions.text: Which statement about verbatim theatre is accurate?

options: Its script is built from the recorded words of real people, often about real events
It is always improvised with no script
It uses only movement and no spoken words
It must be performed in half-masks

questions.solution: Verbatim theatre uses the real words of real people, taken from interviews, trials or records
questions.hint: Think about what 'verbatim' means

questions.text: Which statement about Frantic Assembly is accurate?

options: It was founded in Moscow by Stanislavski
It created epic theatre in 1920s Germany
It is a British company known for physical theatre that combines movement, text and design
It only performs plays in half-masks

questions.solution: Frantic Assembly is a British physical theatre company that blends movement with text, music and design
questions.hint: Think about the exercises it is known for

questions.text: Compare how Stanislavski and Brecht wanted their audiences to respond to a performance.

rubric.model_answer: Stanislavski wanted the audience to believe in the characters and feel with them, so actors used techniques such as the magic if and emotion memory to create a truthful illusion behind the 'fourth wall'. Brecht wanted the opposite: through the alienation effect, such as direct address, placards and songs, he kept the audience emotionally distanced so they would think critically and see that society could change.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: Stanislavski wanted belief and empathy
1 mark: a Stanislavski technique linked to this (e.g. magic if, emotion memory, fourth wall)
1 mark: Brecht wanted critical thinking and distance
1 mark: a Brecht technique linked to this (e.g. direct address, placards, songs, multi-role)
1 mark: a clear comparison of the two aims

questions.solution: Stanislavski aimed for belief and empathy; Brecht aimed for critical distance
questions.hint: Start with what each wanted the audience to feel or think

questions.text: Which vocal skill describes how high or low a voice sounds?

options: Pitch
Pace
Pause
Projection
feedback: Pace is the speed of speech
A pause is a silence or break
Projection is making the voice carry to the back of the audience

questions.solution: Pitch is how high or low the voice sounds
questions.hint: Think of notes on a musical scale

questions.text: Which vocal skill is the speed at which an actor speaks? Give the term.

feedback.pitch: Pitch is how high or low the voice is
feedback.pause: A pause is a break or silence in speech

questions.solution: Pace is the speed of speech; changing it can show emotions such as panic or calm
questions.hint: It is a four-letter word beginning with P

questions.text: What is proxemics in drama?

options: The use of space and distance between characters to show their relationship
The rise and fall of the voice
The speed of an actor's movement
The way an actor uses facial expressions

questions.solution: Proxemics is the use of space and distance on stage to show relationships
questions.hint: The word is linked to 'proximity', meaning closeness

questions.text: Which drama technique has an actor stay in character and answer questions from the group about their character's life and feelings? Give the term.

feedback.thought tracking: Thought tracking is speaking a character's thoughts aloud during a freeze

questions.solution: In hot seating an actor answers questions in role to explore the character
questions.hint: The actor sits in a special chair to be questioned

questions.text: What is a still image, also called a tableau or freeze frame?

options: A spoken thought during a pause
A frozen picture made with bodies to show a moment
A sound collage made with voices
A quick change of costume

questions.solution: A still image is a frozen picture, made by the performers' bodies, that captures a moment
questions.hint: Think about what 'freeze' means

questions.text: Which physical skill describes the way a character walks?

options: Gait
Gesture
Posture
Proxemics
feedback: A gesture is a movement of part of the body, such as the hands
Posture is how the body is held
Proxemics is the use of space between characters

questions.solution: Gait is the way a person walks, for example limping, striding or shuffling
questions.hint: It is a short word that sounds like a garden entrance

questions.text: Which vocal skill means making the voice carry clearly to the back of the auditorium without shouting? Give the term.

feedback.volume: Volume is simply how loud; carrying the voice clearly without shouting has its own name

questions.solution: Projection carries the voice to the whole audience, supported by breath from the diaphragm, without shouting
questions.hint: Think of 'throwing' the voice forward to the back row

questions.text: What is the difference between pitch and tone?

options: Pitch is how fast the voice is; tone is how loud it is
Pitch is the accent; tone is the pause before a line
Pitch is the emotion in the voice; tone is how high or low it is
Pitch is how high or low the voice is; tone is the emotion or attitude in it

questions.solution: Pitch is high or low; tone shows feeling or attitude, such as sarcastic, warm or angry
questions.hint: One is about musical height, the other about feeling

questions.text: What is the difference between gesture and posture?

options: A gesture is how the body is held; posture is a movement of the hands
A gesture is a way of walking; posture is a facial expression
A gesture is a vocal sound; posture is the distance between actors
A gesture is a movement of part of the body to communicate; posture is how the body is held
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: A gesture is a movement such as a wave or a point; posture is the way the body is held, such as hunched or upright
questions.hint: One is a movement, the other is a position

questions.text: During a freeze, an actor steps forward and speaks their character's private thoughts aloud. What is this technique called? Give the term.

feedback.hot seating: Hot seating is answering questions in role
feedback.aside: An aside is a quick remark to the audience during the action, not in a freeze
feedback.soliloquy: A soliloquy is a speech by a character alone on stage, not a rehearsal technique in a freeze

questions.solution: Thought tracking reveals a character's inner thoughts during a freeze
questions.hint: The technique 'tracks' what is going on in the character's mind

questions.text: Which term describes a short remark made directly to the audience that the other characters on stage do not hear?

options: Soliloquy
Monologue
Dialogue
Aside
feedback: A soliloquy is a longer speech by a character alone on stage
A monologue is a long speech by one character, often heard by others on stage
Dialogue is conversation between characters

questions.solution: An aside is a brief comment to the audience that other characters on stage do not hear
questions.hint: The actor turns 'to the side' to share it

questions.text: What is the difference between a soliloquy and a monologue?

options: A soliloquy shares private thoughts, usually alone on stage; a monologue is a long speech, often to others
A soliloquy is a short remark; a monologue is a song
A soliloquy is spoken to other characters; a monologue is always spoken alone
There is no difference: both words mean an aside

questions.solution: In a soliloquy a character, usually alone, speaks their thoughts; a monologue is any long speech by one character
questions.hint: Think about whether anyone else is listening

questions.text: Which vocal skill is a deliberate silence or break in speech, used to build tension or show thought? Give the term.

feedback.pace: Pace is the speed of speech; a silence is something else

questions.solution: A pause is a deliberate silence that can build tension or show a character thinking
questions.hint: It is the opposite of speaking continuously

questions.text: Which physical skill uses the face to show feelings, such as a frown or a raised eyebrow? Give the term.

feedback.gesture: A gesture uses the hands, arms or head; this skill uses the face

questions.solution: Facial expression shows a character's feelings through the face
questions.hint: Think about which part of the body is used

questions.text: An actor playing an old king who has just lost his power stands with rounded shoulders and a lowered head. Which physical skill is the actor mainly using?

options: Projection
Pitch
Pace
Posture
feedback: Projection is a vocal skill
Pitch is a vocal skill
Pace is a vocal skill

questions.solution: Posture is how the body is held; rounded shoulders and a lowered head suggest defeat
questions.hint: Projection, pitch and pace are vocal skills

questions.text: Two characters who have just argued stand at opposite ends of the stage, as far apart as possible. Which skill is the director using to show their relationship?

options: Proxemics
Intonation
Thought tracking
Hot seating

questions.solution: Proxemics uses distance on stage; the large gap shows the rift between them
questions.hint: Think about the space between the actors

questions.text: As her character starts to panic, an actor says her lines faster and faster. Which vocal skill is she changing? Give the term.

feedback.pitch: Pitch is how high or low the voice is
feedback.pause: A pause is a silence; here she is speeding up

questions.solution: Increasing the pace of speech shows rising panic
questions.hint: Think about how quickly the words come out

questions.text: In rehearsal, the class makes two lines facing each other. A character walks between them while each person speaks advice or warnings about a decision. What is this technique?

options: Hot seating
Role on the wall
Marking the moment
Conscience alley

questions.solution: Conscience alley (also called decision alley) voices the arguments a character weighs up before a choice
questions.hint: The two lines form a narrow path the character walks down

questions.text: To explore a character, a group draws the outline of a body, writing facts about the character outside it and their feelings inside. What is this technique called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Role on the wall records what is known about a character outside the outline and their inner feelings inside
questions.hint: The outline is usually stuck up for the whole group to see

questions.text: A group freezes at the most important moment of a scene, then adds a spotlight and slow motion to draw the audience's attention to it. Which technique is this?

options: Cross-cutting
Conscience alley
Marking the moment
Hot seating

questions.solution: Marking the moment highlights a key moment so the audience notices its importance
questions.hint: The group is drawing attention to one key moment

questions.text: Read this stage direction: 'Sam whispers, but the whole audience must hear every word.' Which pair of vocal skills must the actor balance?

options: Pitch and gait
Volume and projection
Pace and posture
Accent and gesture

questions.solution: A whisper needs low volume, but good projection and clear diction let it reach the back row
questions.hint: Gait, posture and gesture are physical skills, not vocal ones

questions.text: Read this stage direction: 'Jo moves slowly towards her brother until they are nose to nose.' What does the change in proxemics most likely show?

options: Jo has forgotten her lines
The tension or closeness between them is increasing
The scene has moved to a new location
Jo is speaking directly to the audience

questions.solution: Closing the distance between characters shows growing tension or intimacy
questions.hint: Proxemics is about distance: what does closing the gap suggest?

questions.text: Read this: 'Two scenes, a kitchen and a classroom, are set up on stage at the same time, and the action cuts back and forth between them like editing in a film.' What is this drama technique called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Cross-cutting switches the action back and forth between two or more scenes on stage
questions.hint: The name comes from film editing

questions.text: Read this rehearsal note: 'Lower your pitch, slow your pace and stand tall.' What kind of character is the actor most likely being directed to play?

options: A calm, authoritative figure
A frightened young child
A panicking messenger
A giggling friend

questions.solution: A low pitch, slow pace and upright posture suggest calm authority and high status
questions.hint: Work out what each of the three notes suggests, then combine them

questions.text: A director wants the audience to hear what three characters are privately thinking at the same moment, without the characters speaking to each other. Which technique would do this most directly?

options: Thought tracking
Hot seating
Proxemics
Projection
feedback: Hot seating is questioning a character, usually in rehearsal
Proxemics is about the space between characters, not their thoughts
Projection is a vocal skill, not a way to reveal thoughts

questions.solution: Thought tracking lets each character in a freeze speak their private thoughts to the audience
questions.hint: Which technique reveals inner thoughts during a freeze?

questions.text: Explain how an actor could use two vocal skills to show that a character is furious.

rubric.model_answer: The actor could raise the volume and use a sharp, harsh tone, so the anger is clearly heard. They could also increase the pace, speaking quickly with sudden emphasis on key words, which shows the character losing control.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first vocal skill named (e.g. volume, tone, pace, pitch, emphasis)
1 mark: how it would be used to show fury
1 mark: second vocal skill named
1 mark: how it would be used to show fury

questions.solution: Volume, tone, pace, pitch and emphasis can all be used to show anger
questions.hint: Choose two vocal skills, then describe exactly how each would sound

questions.text: Which statement about projection is accurate?

options: Projection means speaking as quickly as possible
Projection is only needed in very small studio theatres
Projection means changing accent to suit a character
Good projection makes the voice carry to the back of the space, supported by breath, without shouting
feedback: That describes pace
Projection matters most in large spaces, where the voice must reach the back row
Changing accent is a separate vocal choice

questions.solution: Projection uses breath support so the voice reaches the whole audience without strain or shouting
questions.hint: Think about the back row of a large theatre

questions.text: Why might a director use hot seating during rehearsals rather than in the final performance?

options: It is the main way to show a set change to the audience
It deepens the actor's understanding of the character's background and motives
It replaces the need to learn lines
It tests whether the lighting rig works

questions.solution: Hot seating is an exploratory technique: answering questions in role builds a fuller understanding of the character
questions.hint: Think about what the actor learns by answering questions in role

questions.text: A director says: 'Use levels to show status in this scene.' Which choice follows this note most clearly?

options: The king stands on a raised platform while the servants kneel below him
The king speaks more quietly than the servants
The king wears a red costume
The king exits stage left

questions.solution: Levels means height on stage; placing the king high and the servants low shows his higher status
questions.hint: 'Levels' refers to height

questions.text: Which statement about still images (freeze frames) is accurate?

options: They must always include spoken dialogue
They can show a key moment clearly, using levels, facial expression and proxemics
They can only be used at the very end of a play
They are a lighting effect, not an acting technique

questions.solution: Still images freeze a moment; levels, facial expression and proxemics make its meaning clear
questions.hint: Think about which skills still work when nobody moves or speaks

questions.text: An actor is told her lines sound flat and monotonous. Which change to her vocal skills would most directly fix this?

options: Speak at exactly the same speed throughout
Stand completely still
Vary her pitch and intonation
Make every pause the same length

questions.solution: A flat delivery lacks variety; varying pitch and intonation brings the lines to life
questions.hint: 'Flat' describes a voice that hardly rises or falls

questions.text: Explain how proxemics and posture could be used together to show that one character is more powerful than another.

rubric.model_answer: The powerful character could stand upright and open, taking up space centre stage, while the weaker character is hunched and closed. Using proxemics, the powerful character could move towards the other and invade their space, while the weaker one backs away towards the edge of the stage, so the audience sees who controls the space.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: posture of the powerful character
1 mark: posture of the weaker character
1 mark: use of distance and space (proxemics)
1 mark: how the audience reads status from these choices

questions.solution: Upright, open posture and control of space show power; hunched posture and retreating show weakness
questions.hint: Think about how each character holds their body and who controls the space

questions.text: What is the name of the thin metal disc with a pattern cut into it, placed in a lantern to project shapes such as leaves or a window? Give the term.

feedback.gel: A gel changes the colour of the light, not its shape

questions.solution: A gobo is a cut-out stencil placed in a profile lantern to project a shape or pattern
questions.hint: It is a short word beginning with G

questions.text: What is a gel in stage lighting?

options: A coloured filter placed in front of a lantern
A metal stencil that projects a pattern
A rotating section of stage floor
A large cloth at the back of the stage
feedback: That is a gobo
That is a revolve
That is a cyclorama

questions.solution: A gel is a sheet of coloured filter that changes the colour of a lantern's light
questions.hint: Think about how designers change the colour of light

questions.text: What is a cyclorama?

options: A rotating section of the stage floor
A large cloth or screen at the back of the stage, often lit to suggest sky or mood
A lantern with a soft-edged beam
A list of the costumes for each character

questions.solution: A cyclorama (cyc) is a large backcloth or screen, often lit in colour to suggest sky or atmosphere
questions.hint: It is usually at the very back of the stage

questions.text: Which type of stage lantern gives a soft-edged beam and has a stepped lens? Give the name.

feedback.profile: A profile spot gives a hard-edged beam and can take a gobo
feedback.profile spot: A profile spot gives a hard-edged beam and can take a gobo

questions.solution: A fresnel has a stepped lens that gives a soft-edged beam, useful for washes of light
questions.hint: It is named after a French physicist who designed the stepped lens

questions.text: In theatre, what are props?

options: The wooden frames that hold up the scenery
The lanterns hung above the audience
The written cues in the prompt book
Objects used on stage by the actors or to dress the set

questions.solution: Props (short for properties) are objects used by actors or placed to dress the set
questions.hint: The word is short for 'properties'

questions.text: What is a flat in set design?

options: A lightweight frame covered in canvas or board, painted to form walls
A rotating section of the floor
A coloured filter for a lantern
A soft-edged spotlight

questions.solution: Flats are lightweight frames covered with canvas or board, painted and joined to make walls
questions.hint: Think of the walls of a room on stage

questions.text: What is the term for music played quietly underneath dialogue or action to create mood? Give the term.
questions.solution: Underscoring is music played beneath dialogue or action to build mood
questions.hint: The music sits beneath the scene

questions.text: What is the difference between a fresnel and a profile spot?

options: A fresnel gives a soft-edged beam; a profile gives a hard-edged beam that can be shaped
A fresnel gives a hard-edged beam; a profile gives a soft-edged beam
A fresnel is a sound effect; a profile is a lighting effect
A fresnel lights the audience; a profile lights the foyer
feedback: You have swapped them round

questions.solution: Fresnels give soft-edged washes; profiles give hard-edged beams that can be shaped with shutters or gobos
questions.hint: Think about which lantern can project a sharp gobo pattern

questions.text: What is the difference between a blackout and a fade?

options: A blackout always happens slowly; a fade is always instant
A blackout turns all the stage lights off, often instantly; a fade changes the lighting gradually
A blackout uses coloured gels; a fade uses gobos
A blackout lights only the cyclorama; a fade lights only the actors

questions.solution: A blackout leaves the stage in darkness, usually suddenly; a fade changes the light gradually over time
questions.hint: Think about how quickly each change happens

questions.text: What is the name of the drawing that shows the layout of a set from above, including where furniture and entrances are? Give the term.
questions.solution: A ground plan shows the set from above, with furniture, entrances and the audience marked
questions.hint: It shows the set as if you were looking straight down from above

questions.text: Which colour of light would a designer most likely use to suggest a cold winter night?

options: Amber
Red
Blue
Orange

questions.solution: Cool blue light is a common convention for night and cold
questions.hint: Amber, red and orange are warm colours

questions.text: Which lantern is aimed by an operator to follow a performer around the stage? Give the name.
questions.solution: A follow spot is operated by hand so its beam can track a performer
questions.hint: An operator moves it by hand to 'chase' the actor

questions.text: What is a costume designer mainly responsible for?

options: Designing what the actors wear, including accessories
Designing the colour and angle of the lighting
Building and painting the set
Writing the sound cues for the show

questions.solution: The costume designer designs the clothing and accessories that show character, period and status
questions.hint: Think about the word 'costume'

questions.text: What is the name for a platform used to create different levels on stage? Give the term.
questions.solution: A rostrum (plural rostra) is a platform used to build levels on stage
questions.hint: It is a Latin word beginning with R; its plural ends in -a

questions.text: A designer wants leafy shadows to dapple the stage floor during a forest scene. What should she put into a profile lantern?

options: Gel
Barn doors
Gauze
Gobo
feedback: A gel changes colour, not pattern
Barn doors are flaps that shape the edge of a fresnel's beam
A gauze is a fabric screen, not something placed in a lantern

questions.solution: A gobo with a leaf pattern projects dappled leafy shadows
questions.hint: She needs to change the shape of the light, not its colour

questions.text: A scene is set at sunset. Which lighting choice suits it?

options: Cold blue light from directly above
Bright white strobe light
Warm amber and orange light, low from the side
Green light from below

questions.solution: Sunset light is warm and low, so amber or orange light from a low side angle suggests it
questions.hint: Think about the colour and angle of the real sun in the evening

questions.text: A ghost appears behind a thin fabric screen when lit from behind, then vanishes when only the front of the screen is lit. What is this type of fabric called? Give the term.
questions.solution: A gauze (scrim) looks solid when lit from the front and see-through when the area behind it is lit
questions.hint: The fabric looks solid when lit from the front

questions.text: A play needs to change quickly from a kitchen to a garden and back many times. Which piece of staging would let a whole room spin round to reveal the other location?

options: Trap door
Revolve
Cyclorama
Gobo

questions.solution: A revolve rotates to swap one set for another quickly
questions.hint: The room needs to turn round

questions.text: A character must change from a maid's uniform into a ball gown in under a minute backstage. What is a very fast costume change like this called? Give the term.
questions.solution: A quick change uses hidden fastenings and pre-set costumes so an actor can change in seconds
questions.hint: The name describes how fast it happens

questions.text: A designer wants a ghost to rise suddenly through the floor of the stage. Which feature of the stage would make this possible?

options: Fly tower
Cyclorama
Apron
Trap door in the stage floor

questions.solution: A trap is an opening in the stage floor through which actors or objects can appear
questions.hint: The ghost comes up from below

questions.text: Read this design note: 'Lantern 4: profile spot, blue gel, window gobo, focused on the bed.' What will the audience see?

options: A soft red wash over the whole stage
A spotlight following an actor around the stage
A coloured cloth hanging at the back of the stage
A blue, window-shaped pattern of light on the bed

questions.solution: The gel makes the light blue, the gobo shapes it like a window, and it is focused on the bed
questions.hint: Work out what the gel does, then what the gobo does

questions.text: Read this cue sheet (LX = lighting cue, SFX = sound effect cue): 'LX 12: 5-second fade to blackout. SFX 7: thunder, loud.' What happens?

options: The lights snap off instantly while soft music plays
A spotlight follows an actor while rain falls on stage
The lights fade to darkness over five seconds and a loud thunder sound plays
Sound effect 12 plays for five seconds

questions.solution: LX 12 fades the lights to darkness over 5 seconds; SFX 7 plays loud thunder
questions.hint: Read the lighting cue first, then the sound cue

questions.text: Read this: 'The sound of rain starts in the speaker on the left and moves to the speaker on the right, so it seems to travel across the stage.' What is this sound technique called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Panning moves a sound between speakers so it seems to travel across the space
questions.hint: The same word describes turning a camera from side to side

questions.text: A costume designer dresses a rich character in a crisp, well-fitted suit and a poor character in a faded, patched coat. What is the designer mainly communicating?

options: The characters' status and wealth
The time of day
The weather in the scene
The characters' ages

questions.solution: The condition and fit of costumes show differences in status and wealth
questions.hint: Compare the condition of the two costumes

questions.text: A designer chooses a minimalist set: a bare stage with one chair and a single hanging light bulb. What effect is this choice most likely to have?

options: It recreates a fully detailed, realistic room
It focuses attention on the actors and can suggest emptiness or isolation
It makes the exact location clear in every detail
It allows many scene changes using flats

questions.solution: A minimalist set strips away detail, focusing attention on the actors and suggesting mood rather than a real place
questions.hint: Think about what the audience looks at when there is almost nothing on stage

questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use colour and angle to create a frightening atmosphere.

rubric.model_answer: The designer could use cold colours, such as blue or green gels, to create an unnatural, eerie mood. Lighting the actors from below would throw strange shadows upwards across their faces, making them look distorted and threatening, while leaving much of the stage in darkness so the audience cannot see everything.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a colour choice (e.g. cold blue, green, deep red)
1 mark: the effect of the colour on the atmosphere
1 mark: an angle or position (e.g. from below, from the side, backlight)
1 mark: the effect of the angle (e.g. shadows, distortion, silhouette)

questions.solution: Cold or unnatural colours and unusual angles such as uplighting create fear
questions.hint: Deal with colour first, then think about where the light comes from

questions.text: Which statement about a box set is accurate?

options: It is a set made only of cardboard boxes
It is a set designed for in-the-round staging
It is a bare stage with no scenery
It shows a realistic room with three walls, the missing fourth wall facing the audience

questions.solution: A box set is a realistic interior with three walls; the audience looks in through the missing fourth wall
questions.hint: Think of a room with one wall taken away

questions.text: Why might a set designer build a scale model box before the set is made?

options: Because the model is used on stage during the performance
So the audience can buy it in the foyer
So the director and team can see and plan the design in three dimensions before building
Because lanterns are focused using the model

questions.solution: A model box lets the whole team see and test the design in three dimensions before money is spent on building
questions.hint: Think about planning before building

questions.text: Which statement about sound design is accurate?

options: Sound design only means choosing music for the interval
Sound effects must always be recorded, never live
Sound can establish location, time and mood, and can be live or recorded
Sound is only used in musicals

questions.solution: Sound design can set location, time and mood, using live or recorded sound
questions.hint: Think of all the jobs sound can do in a play

questions.text: A designer must show a play set in three different locations without any scene changes. Which kind of set would allow this?

options: Composite set showing all three locations on stage at once
Box set of a single room
Cyclorama with no scenery
Single flat at the back of the stage

questions.solution: A composite set shows several locations on stage at the same time, so no scene changes are needed
questions.hint: All three places need to be visible at the same time

questions.text: Why do costume designers often attach fabric swatches to their design drawings?

options: To prove the costume has been worn before
To show the colour, texture and weight of the materials to be used
To show the lighting cues
To record where actors stand on stage

questions.solution: Swatches show the real colour, texture and weight of fabric, which a drawing cannot fully show
questions.hint: Think about what a drawing cannot show

questions.text: Explain how a set designer could show time passing between the beginning and the end of a play set in the same room.

rubric.model_answer: The designer could age the room: at the start it is clean and tidy with new furniture; by the end the wallpaper is faded and peeling, the furniture is worn and dust sheets cover some objects. Small changes such as a calendar, a different season through the window or a dying plant would also show time passing without changing the layout.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a valid change to the set (e.g. wear, decay, new objects)
1 mark: a second valid change
1 mark: how the audience reads time passing from the changes
1 mark: practical design detail (e.g. same layout, set dressing, view through a window)

questions.solution: Ageing the room, changing set dressing and showing a different season all suggest time passing
questions.hint: Think about how a real room changes over many years
